“Hindbrain, hypothalamic and corticolimbic circuits integrate information about food, energy balance, and adiposity to control feeding, energy expenditure and energy balance.
the brain regulates body weight by integrating information from the gut, adipose tissue and the reward circuit to control feeding and energy expenditure.
the brain circuits that control food intake, body weight and energy expenditure are modulated by adiposity and satiety hormones.
In summary, our research is concerned with
elucidating the neural mechanisms of energy balance regulation and body weight homeostasis.
understanding the neural mechanisms underlying the regulation of energy balance.
the neural circuits and signaling pathways that regulate energy balance, food intake and body weight.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain regulates body weight through multiple neural circuits that are modulated by adiposity and satiety hormones.
the brain controls food intake, energy expenditure, and body weight through a complex network of interconnected circuits and signaling pathways.
the brain regulates energy balance and body fat by controlling food intake, food reward and energy expenditure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are trying to understand how the brain regulates food intake and body weight, and what goes wrong in obesity.
the central nervous system is a major regulator of energy balance and that defects in the central regulation of feeding, reward and energy expenditure contribute to the development of obesity.
obesity is a complex disease with a variety of causes and that it is unlikely to be treated by one drug that targets a single molecular pathway.
The main takeaway from our work is that

satiety and leptin signaling and the hypothalaminic circuits are important for the control of food intake and body weight, and that the corticolimboc mesolimbic reward circuits and BAT activity are important for the hedonic properties of foods and for energy expenditure.
the homeostatic and the hedonic systems are integrated and interact in the brain to control food intake and energy balance.
satiety and energy expenditure are regulated by the same set of hormones and neural circuits, which are also involved in the regulation of food intake.
